reference.source: GeneReviews / Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: The condition is defined by asymmetric overgrowth of one side or region of the body in the absence of another recognised overgrowth syndrome
It carries an increased risk of embryonal tumours in childhood, most importantly Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma
Because of this tumour predisposition, structured surveillance with regular abdominal ultrasound and measurement of serum alpha-fetoprotein through early childhood is recommended
It lies on a molecular spectrum with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and many cases relate to mosaic epigenetic or genetic changes at the imprinted 11p15 region
The overgrowth may involve limbs, trunk, or face and can cause leg-length discrepancy requiring orthopaedic assessment
Diagnosis is clinical but warrants investigation to exclude a defined syndrome, including molecular testing of the 11p15 region where appropriate, ideally on affected tissue given mosaicism
Management combines cancer surveillance, orthopaedic monitoring of asymmetry, and genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Isolated hemihyperplasia represents regional overgrowth thought to arise most often from post-zygotic mosaicism, so that a subset of cells carries a growth-promoting genetic or epigenetic alteration while others do not, producing asymmetry. A large proportion of cases involve mosaic disturbances of the imprinted gene cluster on chromosome 11p15, the same region implicated in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, which explains both the overlapping phenotype and the shared predisposition to embryonal tumours such as Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma. The mosaic nature accounts for the variable distribution of overgrowth and for the frequently negative results of testing performed on blood rather than affected tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome and vascular overgrowth disorders
Limb hypertrophy from arteriovenous malformation or chronic inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Regular abdominal ultrasound surveillance for Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma through the high-risk years
Serial serum alpha-fetoprotein measurement for hepatoblastoma detection
Molecular testing of the 11p15 imprinting region, preferably on affected tissue given mosaicism
Clinical photography and measurement to document and monitor asymmetry
Orthopaedic assessment including leg-length evaluation and imaging where indicated
Genetic review to exclude a defined overgrowth syndrome
redFlags: A palpable abdominal mass or haematuria suggesting Wilms tumour
A rising alpha-fetoprotein or hepatic mass suggesting hepatoblastoma
Rapidly progressive or disproportionate overgrowth suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Significant, worsening leg-length discrepancy affecting gait and posture
reference.prognosis: For most children the outlook is good, with the principal risks being childhood embryonal tumours during the surveillance window and the functional impact of limb asymmetry. Early tumour detection through surveillance substantially improves outcomes, and the excess cancer risk falls markedly after early childhood.
pitfalls: Failing to institute or maintain tumour surveillance during the vulnerable early years
Relying on blood-based molecular testing and being falsely reassured when the change is mosaic and tissue-limited
Overlooking features that would reclassify the child as having Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Neglecting orthopaedic follow-up for progressive leg-length discrepancy
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
